metadata.title: AI Planning And Search Foundations - Sources
metadata.description: Primary references for state-space search, heuristic search, CSPs, adversarial search, classical planning, HTN, belief-state planning, and planner-agent integration.

textbooks.name: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach
textbooks.description: Russell & Norvig. Canonical AI textbook for state-space search, informed search, CSPs, adversarial search, planning, uncertainty, and agent task environments.

textbooks.name: Artificial Intelligence: Foundations of Computational Agents
textbooks.description: Poole & Mackworth. Open textbook covering search, constraint satisfaction, planning, knowledge representation, and decision making.

software_and_specs.name: AIMA Python
software_and_specs.description: Reference implementations accompanying Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, including search, games, CSPs, and planning examples.

software_and_specs.name: Fast Downward Planning System
software_and_specs.description: Research planning system for classical planning. Useful as a reference point for PDDL-style planning and heuristic search in planning domains.

software_and_specs.name: Planning.wiki PDDL Reference
software_and_specs.description: Practical reference for PDDL domain/problem syntax and planning constructs.

software_and_specs.name: OR-Tools CP-SAT Solver
software_and_specs.description: Google OR-Tools documentation for constraint programming with CP-SAT; useful when CSP modeling should become executable solver work.

software_and_specs.name: AIPlan4EU Unified Planning Library
software_and_specs.description: Python library for specifying classical, numeric, and temporal planning problems and dispatching them to multiple back-end planners (including Fast Downward) through one API. Practical entry point when a project needs a planner as a tool rather than a research build.

papers.name: A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths
papers.description: Hart, Nilsson & Raphael (1968). Foundational A* paper establishing heuristic search for minimum-cost paths.

papers.name: STRIPS: A New Approach to the Application of Theorem Proving to Problem Solving
papers.description: Fikes & Nilsson (1971). Original STRIPS paper for symbolic action preconditions and effects in automated planning.

papers.name: Efficient Selectivity and Backup Operators in Monte-Carlo Tree Search
papers.description: Coulom (2006), Computers and Games CG 2006, LNCS 4630, pp. 72-83. Foundational Monte Carlo Tree Search reference for high-branching game-tree search. 2026-07-11 correction: the DOI previously recorded here (10.1007/11871842_29) actually resolves to Kocsis & Szepesvari's UCT paper below, not to this one — corrected to Coulom's own DOI.

papers.name: Bandit Based Monte-Carlo Planning
papers.description: Kocsis & Szepesvari (2006), Machine Learning: ECML 2006, LNCS 4212, pp. 282-293. Introduces UCT, the UCB1-based tree policy Q(s,a) + c*sqrt(ln(N(s))/N(s,a)) that most modern MCTS implementations use for selection. Referenced in Primitive #6.

papers.name: Agentic LLM Planning via Step-Wise PDDL Simulation: An Empirical Characterisation
papers.description: Göbel, Lorang, Zips & Glück (arXiv:2603.06064, 2026). Evaluates LLM-as-search-policy over MCP-exposed PDDL simulators (PyPDDLEngine) on 102 IPC Blocksworld instances under a 180-second budget: agentic Claude Haiku 4.5 reaches 66.7% vs 63.7% direct, at 5.7 times token cost per solved instance (5.97 times per run), versus 85.3% Fast Downward. Study-specific results, sections III-C, IV-B and IV-C; verified from primary full text. Referenced in Primitive #10.

papers.name: Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code
papers.description: Corrêa, Pereira & Seipp (arXiv:2503.18809, 2025). An LLM generates several domain-dependent Python heuristic functions, selected by training-task performance within a greedy best-first search; the resulting heuristics solve more unseen test tasks than state-of-the-art domain-independent heuristics for classical planning, using an unoptimized Python planner against optimized C++ baselines. Treat LLM-generated heuristics as inadmissible by default. Referenced in Primitive #3.

papers.name: Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
papers.description: Kambhampati et al., ICML 2024 (PMLR v235). Position paper arguing autoregressive LLMs cannot plan or self-verify, but are useful as approximate knowledge sources inside a generate-critique-repair loop wrapped by sound external verifiers. Companion evaluation of the compound architecture in arXiv:2411.14484 (2024). Source of the verifier-loop guidance in Primitive #10.

papers.name: LLMs as Planning Formalizers: A Survey for Leveraging Large Language Models to Construct Automated Planning Models
papers.description: Tantakoun, Zhu & Muise (arXiv:2503.18971, submitted March 2025, revised October 2025). Survey of the neuro-symbolic pattern in which LLMs translate natural language into formal planning models for sound off-the-shelf planners, rather than emitting plans directly. Grounds the 'LLM as formalizer, not planner' guidance in Primitive #7.

papers.name: Can LLM-Reasoning Models Replace Classical Planning? A Benchmark Study
papers.description: Goebel & Zips (arXiv:2507.23589, July 2025). Systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art language models prompted directly with PDDL domain and problem files, measured against Fast Downward. Models are competent on simple tasks and degrade on complex ones, with weaknesses concentrated in resource management, state tracking, and constraint compliance; the authors recommend hybrid LLM-plus-classical-planner architectures rather than replacement. Referenced in Primitive #7.

papers.name: Using Large Language Models for Embodied Planning Introduces Systematic Safety Risks
papers.description: Zhang, Qu, Li, Wu, Hutter, Li & Shi (arXiv:2604.18463, April 2026; revised May 2026). Introduces DESPITE, a 12,279-task embodied-planning benchmark covering physical and normative dangers with deterministic validation, across 23 models. The best-planning model fails to produce a valid plan on 0.4% of tasks but produces dangerous plans on 28.3%; across open-source models 3B-671B, planning ability scales 0.4%-99.3% while safety awareness stays roughly flat at 38-57%. Primary evidence that plan validity and plan safety are independent axes. Referenced in Primitive #7 and the Validity Gate Vs Safety Gate pattern.

papers.name: Tree Search for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.description: Ji, Ma, Wang, Chen, Chu & Wu (arXiv:2509.21240, September 2025; revised March 2026), ICLR 2026. Tree-GRPO branches agent rollouts from shared prefixes, yielding more distinct trajectories per unit compute than independent chain sampling and enabling step-wise process supervision from outcome-only rewards. Source of the prefix-sharing economics note in Primitive #6.

papers.name: Training the Orchestrator: A Supervised Approach to End-to-End PDDL Planning with LLM Agents
papers.description: Mangannavar, Coalson, Dugar & Tadepalli (arXiv:2606.21740, June 2026). HALO distills verifier-certified repair trajectories into a small fine-tuned orchestrator that selects among specialized PDDL repair agents, reported across 11 PDDL domains as matching or exceeding the GPT-5-mini prompted baseline on success rate and sitting within three percentage points of the stronger Gemini-3-Flash, at approximately 45x lower orchestration cost than GPT-5-mini and 15x lower than Gemini-3-Flash per task, with 40-50% fewer LLM calls. Referenced in Primitive #10 as a maturity-stage optimization.

papers.name: LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
papers.description: Valmeekam, Stechly & Kambhampati (arXiv:2409.13373, Sep 2024). o1-preview evaluated on PlanBench: 97.8% zero-shot on Blocksworld, 52.8% zero-shot / 41.6% one-shot on Mystery Blocksworld (obfuscated predicates), 37.3% on Randomized Mystery Blocksworld, and 23.63% on the 110 instances requiring at least 20 steps; identified only 27% of unsolvable instances as true negatives; API cost $42.12 per 100 instances (o1-mini $3.69 per 100) versus Fast Downward's ~0.265s per instance. Part of the dated evidence arc in Primitive #7's benchmark reality check.

papers.name: Frontier Large Language Models Rival State-of-the-Art Planners
papers.description: Corrêa, Pereira & Seipp (arXiv:2511.09378, v1 Nov 2025, v2 May 2026; preprint, no venue). On 360 freshly generated tasks (to mitigate contamination) across 8 IPC-2023 Learning Track domains, all plans checked with VAL: Gemini 3.1 Pro solved 245 with standard descriptions and 231 obfuscated; GPT-5 solved 205 (152 obfuscated); the strongest tested classical planner (Scorpion Maidu, 30-min/8 GiB limit) solved 234. Gemini outperforms the planner on standard descriptions and is competitive when obfuscated. Caveats: on obfuscated tasks the model frequently identifies the underlying PDDL domain from structural cues, and LLM inference uses orders of magnitude more energy than the classical planner. Part of the dated evidence arc in Primitive #7's benchmark reality check.

papers.name: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective Than Scaling Model Parameters
papers.description: Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar (arXiv:2408.03314, Aug 2024). On MATH with a learned process reward model verifier: beam search beats best-of-N at low generation budgets and on medium-difficulty problems consistently across the budget range; best-of-N wins on easy problems at high budgets because beam search over-optimizes the PRM; at the hardest difficulty level neither method makes meaningful progress; lookahead search generally underperforms other methods at matched budget. Source of the compute-matched best-of-N baseline rule in Primitive #6. Difficulty bins are relative to the base model's own pass@1 and do not transfer across verifiers/models without rechecking.
